title: I Didn’t Believe Evolve’s Designer. Then I Rode the CIMA [Review]

takeaways.text: Build niggles: no internal hose guide in the fork steerer or the Kreuza Apex cockpit (a guide wire was needed; about 20 minutes for the bar) and an over-tight steerer compression plug that he had to grind to remove.

The narrow seatpost needs Evolve's 3D-printed holder for a Di2 battery; it still held after about 1,500 km. BSA threaded bottom bracket, flexible one-piece spacers and a locking seatpost wedge are practical touches.

On his scale the size-ML frame weighed 765 g, the uncut fork 385 g and the seatpost 160 g (1,310 g); the Kreuza Apex cockpit added 310 g, and his Ultegra Di2 build with Elitewheels Drive SL 58D wheels and pedals weighed 7.1 kg.
Stack sits about 7 mm above a Winspace SLC5 and 3 mm below a Tarmac SL8; the 74° seat and 73.8° head angles give 57 mm of trail (SLC5: 60.1 mm), so steering feels lively rather than settled.

Felt clearly stiffer than the Winspace SLC5 out of the saddle, with no bottom-bracket give under high torque; slightly less comfortable than the SLC5, though the compliant seatpost closes most of the gap.
Continental GP5000 S TR 32 mm tires measured about 34 mm on wide Elitewheels rims, which he called very close to the physical limit; he would not go wider than the official 32 mm.
Significant toe overlap on his size ML with rearward cleats; riders with size 45+ shoes or forward cleats may get drive-side heel rub where the chainstay flares around the UDH hardware.

At US$2,300 for the frameset (Winspace SLC5 US$2,900, Tarmac SL8 US$3,500) he rated it the better value; it felt as fast as the SLC5 but slower than aero frames such as the M6 or T1600 above about 45 km/h.

disclosure: Evolve supplied the frame for review; the description carries affiliate links to Evolve and Panda Podium and a Cyclists Hub discount page.
summary: About 1,500 km on a size-ML CIMA road frame with Ultegra Di2: weigh-in, build issues, geometry, stiffness and comfort against the Winspace SLC5.
